title: Bharti Airtel Just Overtook HDFC Bank as India’s Second Most Valuable Company. Here’s Why NRI Investors Should Pay Attention.
excerpt: A telecom giant’s 270% five-year surge reshuffles Dalal Street’s pecking order — and signals a deeper shift in what India’s market rewards.
body:
For most of the past decade, India’s market capitalisation leaderboard had a familiar look: Reliance Industries on top, HDFC Bank a comfortable second, and everyone else jostling below. On Monday, May 18, that order broke.

Bharti Airtel’s shares surged 2.6 per cent to an intra-day high of ₹1,953.80 on the BSE, pushing its market capitalisation to ₹11.90 lakh crore and, for the first time, past HDFC Bank’s ₹11.83 lakh crore. By the closing bell, HDFC Bank had clawed back just enough to reclaim second place by a sliver — but the symbolism was unmistakable. India’s largest private-sector bank had been caught, however briefly, by a telecom operator.

## A Five-Year Transformation

The numbers behind Airtel’s ascent are striking. Over the past five years, Bharti Airtel shares have returned roughly 270 per cent, dwarfing HDFC Bank’s 49 per cent gain over the same period. Revenue grew 15.68 per cent year-on-year in the March quarter, driven by tariff hikes, 5G monetisation, and an increasingly profitable Africa business whose EBITDA margin touched 49.5 per cent.

The re-rating reflects a broader market conviction: India’s digital infrastructure is now worth more than its banking plumbing. Airtel’s push into data centres, fibre-to-the-home, and enterprise connectivity has convinced analysts that the company is no longer simply a carrier — it is becoming a platform.

## What Changed at HDFC Bank

The other half of the story is HDFC Bank’s own headwinds. Since its mega-merger with HDFC Limited in July 2023, the combined entity has struggled to digest a legacy mortgage book while maintaining the deposit growth rates the market once took for granted. Concerns over chairman succession planning and regulatory scrutiny on priority-sector lending have further weighed on the stock, which fell 0.4 per cent on Monday even as the broader index held steady.

For foreign institutional investors — who have pulled more than ₹2.19 lakh crore out of Indian equities in 2026 — the bank’s premium valuation looked increasingly hard to justify. FII ownership in Indian blue-chip stocks has fallen to a 14-year low, according to TrustLine Holdings CEO N. ArunaGiri, as global capital rotates toward AI-driven semiconductor plays in Taiwan and South Korea.

## The Diaspora Angle

For the estimated 32 million NRIs who collectively hold significant stakes in Indian equities through portfolio investment schemes, mutual funds, and family demat accounts, the Airtel-HDFC Bank flip matters in practical terms. Telecom and digital services have been one of the few sectors consistently delivering double-digit earnings growth in a year when the Sensex is down roughly 8 per cent year-to-date.

The shift also carries a broader signal. India’s most valuable companies are increasingly those that build and operate digital infrastructure — Reliance Jio, Airtel, Infosys — rather than those that intermediated financial flows. For a diaspora whose professional lives are overwhelmingly in technology, the alignment is notable: the India they invest in is starting to look more like the industry they work in.

## What Comes Next

Analysts at multiple global brokerages have set price targets above ₹2,100 for Airtel, citing growth in enterprise services, data centres, and its non-cellular portfolio. Reliance Industries, at ₹18.06 lakh crore, remains comfortably atop the leaderboard, but the contest for second place is now genuinely live.

Whether the flip endures will depend on execution — Airtel must prove its data centre ambitions translate into margins, not just revenue. But the fact that a telecom company can briefly outvalue India’s largest private bank tells you something fundamental has changed about where India’s economic energy is concentrated. NRI investors, who have long treated HDFC Bank as the default India allocation, may want to revisit that assumption.
